original_question: (Well-known problem). A group G is a unique product group if, for any nonempty finite subsets A, B of G, there exists an element of G which can be written uniquely as ab with a ∈ A and b ∈ B. A group G is locally invariant orderable if G admits a partial order < such that for all g, h ∈ G with h ̸= 1, we have either gh > g or gh−1 > g. Does there exist a unique product group which is not locally invariant orderable?
target_in_paper: Problem 21.34 in the section "New Problems (21st issue, 2026)". It asks whether there exists a unique product group that fails to be locally invariant orderable. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper's target essentially verbatim: it includes the exact two definitions used in the problem, keeps the quantifiers on nonempty finite subsets A and B of G, keeps the condition that h != 1 in the local-invariance clause, and asks the same existence question without adding extra hypotheses. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))
refined_question: Does there exist a group G such that, for every pair of nonempty finite subsets A and B of G, there is an element x in G with a unique factorization x = ab where a is in A and b is in B, but G admits no partial order < satisfying the condition that for every g in G and every nonidentity h in G, at least one of gh > g or gh^{-1} > g holds? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))
justification: The paper presents this as a stand-alone open problem and does not supply additional nearby hypotheses or an equivalent reformulation, so the faithful refinement is to keep the scope exactly as stated and only make the uniqueness clause fully explicit as uniqueness of the pair (a,b). I do not broaden the question to the left-orderable variant, because the paper separately records that older question as Problem 15.49 and notes that it already has a positive existence answer; this confirms that Problem 21.34 is intended as the sharper locally invariant orderability version. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))
